summary: Provides guidelines for allocating OSI NSAP addresses in the Internet. They were the basis for initial deployment of CLNP and helped scale CLNP routing and address administration. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules for handing out addresses for an alternate network design, so they stay organized.

questions: how are osi nsap addresses allocated
what is a routing domain confederation
subtitle: How to hand out OSI network addresses so that routing tables stay small as the Internet grows.

tldr.problem: CLNP was being deployed in the Internet, and it needed guidelines for assigning NSAP addresses that would let routing scale instead of listing every area separately.
tldr.mechanism: Addresses are handed out hierarchically along the real network topology: providers get a prefix, subscriber routing domains get longer prefixes inside it, and areas get longer ones still, so one prefix can stand for many networks.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1629 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1237. It says its guidelines were the basis for the initial deployment of CLNP in the Internet.

today: RFC 1629 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1237. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why NSAP Allocation Needs Guidelines
sections.content:
The Internet was moving toward a multi-protocol environment that includes CLNP, the OSI connectionless network protocol. That needs an OSI lower-layers infrastructure, and part of it is a set of rules for assigning NSAP (network service access point) addresses.

The RFC says its guidelines are quite similar to those proposed for IP address allocation with CIDR in RFC 1519. The main difference is address size: 4 octets for CIDR against 20 octets for CLNP, which allows much more flexibility and scalability. It obsoletes RFC 1237; the changes are described as minor and mostly editorial, plus an updated description of OSI routing standards, a new description of IDRP, European recommendations, and advice on routing domain identifiers.

The document focuses on the technical side, which is mostly about routing, not on the paperwork of registering addresses. It deliberately leaves out how a site lays out its internal topology and how System IDs are assigned (that is covered in RFC 1526).
sections.plainLanguage: A new kind of network address was being used, and someone had to write down how to give them out sensibly. The goal is that the big routers in the middle of the network do not need to remember every single address.

sections.title: The Routing Protocols the Addresses Must Serve
sections.content:
OSI splits routing into three parts: end systems talking to routers (ES-IS), routers inside one routing domain (intra-domain IS-IS) and routing between domains (IDRP). A routing domain is a set of systems under one administration that run common routing protocols.

IS-IS has two levels. A domain is divided into areas. Level 1 routers know their own area and send anything else to a level 2 router. Level 2 routers route on address prefixes and prefer the longest matching prefix. On a broadcast LAN, a pseudonode (represented by an elected designated router) cuts the reported links from n-squared to n.

IDRP lets routers called Boundary Intermediate Systems exchange routes between domains, with no restriction on the inter-domain topology. Domains can be grouped into Routing Domain Confederations (RDCs), which may be nested, disjoint or overlapping, so a sequence of domain identifiers can be replaced by a single confederation identifier. IDRP also supports route aggregation, which shrinks reachability information. Each IDRP message carries a 16-octet digital signature computed with MD-4 for data integrity.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers sort the network into neighborhoods and cities. Local routers know every house in their neighborhood. Bigger routers only need to know which neighborhood an address belongs to, so the address has to say so clearly.

sections.title: The Structure of an NSAP Address
sections.content:
An OSI address has two main parts. The Initial Domain Part (IDP) is standardized by ISO. It holds the Authority and Format Identifier (AFI) and the Initial Domain Identifier (IDI) and names the authority that assigns the rest. The Domain Specific Part (DSP) is assigned by that authority, which may subdivide it further.

For routing, IS-IS reads an address as an area address, a system ID and a one-octet selector (SEL). The ID may be one to eight octets long but must have a single known length in a given routing domain. The area address, which is everything before the ID and SEL, must be globally unique.

As the worked example, the RFC uses the U.S. GOSIP Version 2 layout: AFI 47, IDI 0005, then a DSP Format Identifier (80h), a 3-octet Administrative Authority, 2 reserved octets, a 2-octet Routing Domain, a 2-octet Area, a 6-octet ID and the SEL. The ANSI format under the U.S. Data Country Code (AFI 39, IDI 840) has the same DSP structure, with the administrative authority replaced by a registered numeric organization name. The RFC says the technical considerations are the same whichever is used.
sections.plainLanguage: An address is like country, state, city, street and house number written in a fixed order. Each part has its own job, and the order lets routers read just the first part to know where to send things.

sections.title: Allocating by Topology to Shrink Routing Tables
sections.content:
The core argument is that routing scales only if addresses follow the network's topology. If each area in a domain takes its address from an unrelated authority, the domain must advertise every area address separately. The RFC compares this to routing in the TCP/IP Internet before CIDR. For providers that use no default routes, table size would grow with the number of area addresses worldwide.

The better plan is hierarchical. A provider gets a short prefix, gives each subscriber routing domain a slightly longer prefix, and each subscriber hands out area addresses inside its own prefix. To the outside, a whole domain, or all of a provider's subscribers, becomes one prefix.

The RFC points out who benefits: the provider doing the assigning gains little, while other providers gain a lot because they exchange far fewer routes. It therefore argues for direct providers (such as regionals) assigning prefixes to their subscribers. It sees little case for direct providers taking space from indirect providers (backbones), since the gain is small and direct providers may switch backbones.
sections.plainLanguage: If addresses are given out by town, the mail truck only needs a list of towns. If they are given out at random, it needs a list of every house. So the guidance is to give out addresses by where things actually connect.

sections.title: Multi-Homed, Private and Zero-Homed Domains
sections.content:
A domain attached to more than one provider does not fit a strict hierarchy. The RFC describes four approaches. (1) Give the organization one independent prefix; routing stays simple inside but every provider may need an explicit entry for it. (2) Give it a separate address space per provider connection, with each area using the nearest one; this scales better but backup routes are not automatic and addresses change when connectivity changes. (3) Base its prefix on one provider and have the others be selective about whom they tell. (4) Have providers with many shared customers obtain a third prefix for domains attached to both.

Each option has different costs and different effects on routes taken and on policy. The RFC concludes that no single solution can be mandated and that each provider needs a policy on non-local prefixes.

Private point-to-point links between a few domains can be ignored for allocation, because their routing information is not spread through the Internet. Zero-homed domains, with no external connection, should still use globally unique NSAP addresses so that a domain they link to can tell their addresses apart from others.
sections.plainLanguage: If a house has doors on two streets, it is hard to say which street it belongs to. There are several ways to handle it, and each one is a trade between simple maps and extra work, so the RFC lists them instead of picking one.

sections.title: Changing Addresses When the Network Changes
sections.content:
Topology-based addressing means that moving to a new provider can mean getting a new address. The RFC calls this a natural, inevitable consequence of any routing data abstraction, and advises anticipating future topology, for example when a single-homed domain expects to become multi-homed.

Changing addresses at an instant is not practical. Instead, old and new addresses stay valid for a limited time. IS-IS allows several addresses per area for this purpose, and OSI end systems can learn their area addresses automatically from IS-IS Hello packets or by querying routers. If the ID part is globally unique, an end system can reconfigure its whole address without manual work, though routers still need manual changes.

For traffic sent to the old address, the old and new providers can forward to each other if they are adjacent and cooperative. Otherwise intermediate providers can add special entries, or the old provider can encapsulate the traffic. The RFC expects the old address knowledge to be replaced over weeks or months.
sections.plainLanguage: When you move house, the mail for your old address keeps coming for a while. The post office forwards it until everyone learns the new one, and the same idea is used when a network changes its addresses.

sections.title: The Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that zero-homed and single-homed domains use a single address prefix for the whole domain, that single-homed domains base it on their public provider, and that zero-homed domains use globally unique addresses. It recommends using IDRP's Routing Domain Confederations and route aggregation for the extra levels of hierarchy.

For the U.S., it strongly recommends hierarchical assignment from provider prefixes. Under the GOSIP format, all providers, explicitly including the NSFNET backbone and its regionals, should obtain Administrative Authority identifiers, and single-homed subscribers should be given a Routing Domain value from their provider. Each provider and its subscribers should form a confederation.

For Europe, it recommends the ISO DCC scheme (AFI 38 or 39), with a Country Domain Part split by a Country Format Identifier into classes for very large, intermediate and small organizations. A European NSAP can be from 7 to 20 octets long. Elsewhere, hierarchical formats tied to a national backbone are recommended. For IDRP, a Routing Domain Identifier should be based on the NSAP prefix assigned to the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules of thumb are: give each network one neat block of addresses, get the block from the company you connect through, and keep the blocks lined up with how the networks are actually wired.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that security issues are not discussed in the memo, with one exception: the discussion of IS-IS authentication. That authentication allows a password to be associated with each link, each area and the level 2 subdomain, and a router without the right password may not take part in the matching function. The authentication functions are described as extensible, so that a stronger cryptographic scheme can be added later.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper is about handing out addresses, not about locks. The only lock it talks about is a simple password that routers can use to prove they belong.

viz.caption: FOUR WAYS TO ADDRESS A MULTI-HOMED DOMAIN (SUMMARY OF RFC 1629 SECTION 5.4)

cells: One independent prefix for the organization
Every provider may need an explicit route for it
A separate address space per provider connection
Backup routes are not automatic; addresses change with connectivity
A prefix from one provider, selectively advertised by the others
Direct routing only where providers agree to keep extra routes
A shared prefix for domains attached to two cooperating providers
Providers must obtain and manage extra prefixes
